templates.name: Respond: concede part of the target, rebut the rest (two-part options)
Respond: one text supplies a solution to the other's problem
Agree: shared methodological assumption under a dispute
Respond: critique of the target's framework or standard
Respond: the behavior might be explained without the target's interpretation
Difference: how the two authors view an object, compared on one axis
Respond: counterexample to a 'first', 'only' or 'requires' claim
Respond: limit the degree or scope of the target claim
Respond (Text 1 speaking): Text 2's case fits Text 1's general frame
Agree: shared premise beneath a visible disagreement
Respond: rival hypothesis with evidence the target does not account for

items.passage:
Text 1

Indo-Pacific lionfish, introduced to Atlantic waters during the 1980s, have since spread throughout the Caribbean, where they eat enormous numbers of small reef fishes. On nine coral reefs off New Providence Island in the Bahamas, the biomass of the lionfish’s prey species declined by 65 percent in just two years as lionfish populations expanded. <u>Clearly, lionfish are causing steep declines in native fish populations wherever they have colonized Caribbean reefs.</u>

Text 2

That lionfish can deplete individual reefs of small fishes is well documented; whether such losses accumulate across entire reef systems is less certain. Surveying sixteen reefs along approximately 250 kilometers of the Belize Barrier Reef as lionfish arrived, Serena Hackerott and colleagues detected no measurable effect of lionfish on the density, richness, or composition of prey fishes. At that scale, the researchers suggest, fishing, reef complexity, and other factors may overwhelm any lionfish effect.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the underlined claim in Text 1?
options: By accepting that lionfish have spread widely across the Caribbean since the 1980s but disputing that small reef fishes make up most of their diet
By granting that lionfish can sharply reduce prey fishes on a given reef but doubting that the effect is detectable across a large reef system
By agreeing that lionfish are harming native fishes throughout the Caribbean but arguing that fishing does even more damage to those fishes than lionfish do
By conceding that prey fishes declined on the reefs studied in the Bahamas but suggesting that factors other than lionfish were responsible for that decline
items.explanation: Text 1 moves from local evidence (a 65 percent drop on nine Bahamian reefs) to a sweeping claim that lionfish are driving declines “wherever they have colonized Caribbean reefs.” The author of Text 2 grants the local point (“That lionfish can deplete individual reefs of small fishes is well documented”) but doubts that it scales up, citing a survey of sixteen reefs along “approximately 250 kilometers of the Belize Barrier Reef” that detected “no measurable effect of lionfish.” So the author would accept the reef-level effect while questioning a reef-system-wide one.

A.recipe: D7 half right (right concession, invented rebuttal)
A.why_wrong: Text 2 never questions what lionfish eat; its doubt concerns whether losses on single reefs show up across a large reef system.

C.recipe: D7 half right (wrong concession, twisted detail)
C.why_wrong: Text 2 does not agree that lionfish are harming fishes throughout the Caribbean; that is the claim it doubts. It mentions fishing only as a factor that may swamp a lionfish effect in survey data, not as a greater source of damage.

D.recipe: D2 wrong side (rejects a point the speaker grants)
D.why_wrong: Text 2 does not reinterpret the Bahamas decline; it accepts that lionfish can strip individual reefs and questions only whether such losses add up across a whole reef system.

sources.what: Hackerott et al. 2017, PeerJ 5:e3270: sixteen reefs along about 250 km of the Belize Barrier Reef, 2009 to 2013, before and after invasion; no measurable effect of lionfish on prey fish density, richness or composition; other factors may swamp effects
Text 1 detail: Green et al. 2012, PLOS ONE: nine reefs off New Providence Island, Bahamas, 65 percent decline in prey fish biomass in two years

items.notes: Area: natural science (marine ecology). Concession is the reef-scale effect, rebuttal is the scaling up; distractors recombine halves. Hackerott abstract fetched via Europe PMC (PMID 28560093).

items.passage:
Text 1

Tracking individual honeybees as they forage is notoriously difficult. A departing forager quickly vanishes from view, and the radars used to monitor insects migrating at high altitudes are ineffective near the ground, where reflections from vegetation and terrain obscure the faint echo of a single insect. Conventional radio transmitters, meanwhile, require batteries far too heavy for bees to carry. <u>Consequently, the routes individual bees travel across a landscape have remained largely unknown.</u>

Text 2

Entomologists at Rothamsted Research in England developed a harmonic radar specifically for studying low-flying insects. Each insect carries a transponder weighing only a few milligrams; needing no battery, the device sends back the radar’s signal at double the original frequency. Because the radar detects only that doubled frequency, a tagged insect can be picked out even amid strong reflections from the surrounding landscape, at distances of up to 900 meters.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the underlined portion of Text 1?
options: They would argue that conventional entomological radar can follow foraging bees near the ground as long as the frequency of its own signal is doubled.
They would agree that conventional radio transmitters are too heavy for bees to carry but suggest that lighter batteries would allow such transmitters to track foraging bees.
They would agree that reflections from the ground once hid single insects from radar but claim that a more powerful radar signal now overcomes that problem.
They would suggest that tags returning a distinctive signal make it possible to trace bee routes near the ground that could not previously be followed.
items.explanation: Text 1 explains that bees’ routes have “remained largely unknown” because near the ground “reflections from vegetation and terrain obscure the faint echo of a single insect” and radio transmitters are too heavy. Text 2 describes a solution: a transponder “needing no battery” that “sends back the radar’s signal at double the original frequency,” so that the radar, which “detects only that doubled frequency,” can pick out a tagged insect “even amid strong reflections from the surrounding landscape.” The researchers would therefore say that such tags make tracking individual bees possible.

A.why_wrong: In Text 2 the frequency is doubled by the transponder the insect carries, and the radar listens for that doubled signal; nothing suggests that conventional radar works once its own signal is doubled.

B.recipe: D7 half right (true concession, wrong remedy)
B.why_wrong: Text 2 does treat the weight of the device as a problem, but its answer is a transponder “needing no battery,” not a lighter battery for a radio transmitter.

C.recipe: D7 half right (true concession, twisted mechanism)
C.why_wrong: Text 2 does not rely on a stronger signal: a tagged insect stands out because the radar “detects only that doubled frequency,” which the tag sends back.

sources.what: Riley and Smith 2002, Computers and Electronics in Agriculture (Rothamsted Research): ground clutter masks insects for conventional radar; passive frequency-doubling transponders of 1 to 12 mg, no battery; radar detects the doubled frequency amid clutter; range up to 900 m

items.notes: Area: natural science (entomology, methods). Text 1 is unattributed. Abstract fetched via Europe PMC/OpenAlex. The hardest distractor (A) moves the frequency doubling from the tag to the radar, as CB’s f3c45b4f D moves the dating from the breccia to the fossils.

fixes: hardened B (was killed by 'needing no battery') into a half-right option: true weight concession, wrong remedy (lighter batteries)
hardened C (was killed by 'low-flying insects') into a half-right option: true clutter concession, wrong mechanism (stronger signal); key no longer tied longest

items.passage:
Text 1

Where and when did the Indo-European language family, which stretches from Hindi to Irish, begin? In 2012, Remco Bouckaert and colleagues applied methods from evolutionary biology to basic vocabulary, such as words for body parts and numbers, from 103 ancient and modern languages, estimating how rapidly such words are replaced. Their analysis placed the family’s origin in Anatolia 8,000 to 9,500 years ago, consistent with a spread alongside farming.

Text 2

In 2015, linguists Will Chang, Chundra Cathcart, David Hall, and Andrew Garrett reached a different conclusion using a comparable analysis. They required that well-documented ancient and medieval languages be treated as ancestors of their modern descendants, which, they argue, yields more accurate estimates of how fast vocabulary changes. Thus constrained, their results strongly supported the rival hypothesis that Indo-European languages spread from the Pontic-Caspian steppe beginning roughly 6,500 to 5,500 years ago.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both Bouckaert’s team in Text 1 and Chang’s team in Text 2 would most likely agree with which statement?
options: Rates of change in core vocabulary can indicate roughly when the Indo-European languages began to diverge.
The Indo-European languages most likely spread across Europe and Asia together with the practice of farming.
Treating ancient languages as the ancestors of modern ones makes estimates of the language family’s age less reliable.
Words for body parts and numbers are replaced more quickly than other words in a language’s basic vocabulary.
items.explanation: The teams disagree about where and when Indo-European began, but both reach their answers the same way. Bouckaert’s team dated the family by “estimating how rapidly such words are replaced,” and Chang’s team ran “a comparable analysis” designed to give “more accurate estimates of how fast vocabulary changes.” Both therefore assume that the rate of change in basic vocabulary can be used to date the family’s origin.

B.why_wrong: A spread with farming fits Bouckaert’s Anatolian result, but Chang’s team supports the rival steppe view, so they would reject this statement.

C.why_wrong: Chang’s team argues the opposite: treating ancient languages as ancestors “yields more accurate estimates.” Text 1 says nothing about such a constraint.

D.why_wrong: Text 1 mentions body parts and numbers only as examples of basic vocabulary; neither text compares how quickly those words are replaced with the rate for other words.

sources.what: Bouckaert et al. 2012, Science 337: Bayesian phylogeography of basic vocabulary from 103 ancient and contemporary languages, decisive support for Anatolian origin 8,000 to 9,500 years ago
Chang, Cathcart, Hall and Garrett 2015, Language 91(1): ancestry constraints give more accurate rates of lexical change; result strongly supports the steppe hypothesis (c. 6500 to 5500 BP)

items.notes: Area: social science (historical linguistics). Shared methodological assumption under a dispute (3.1 pattern): both teams date the family from rates of change in basic vocabulary. Abstracts fetched via Europe PMC and OpenAlex.

review.note: subject overlap noted, not fixed: live Inferences w2 (Pagel word-replacement rates) and an FSS item (da Silva and Tehrani folktales) also use Indo-European phylogenies; this is a different study and question

items.passage:
Text 1

Archaeologist V. Gordon Childe’s phrase “Neolithic Revolution” summed up a long-standing view of how agriculture began in the Near East. Once people began sowing and harvesting wild cereals, the view held, harvesting would inadvertently favor plants that retained their seeds, and domesticated crops would emerge within a few centuries at most. Farming, in this account, was not a gradual transition but a decisive break with foraging.

Text 2

Ken-ichi Tanno and George Willcox examined wheat remains from archaeological sites across the Near East, distinguishing ears that shatter at maturity, dispersing their seeds as wild wheat does, from ears that remain intact. Although cultivation of wild wheat probably began around 10,500 years ago, nonshattering domesticated forms appeared only around 9,500 years ago, and shattering forms remained common in cultivated fields some 2,000 years later.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would Tanno and Willcox (Text 2) most likely respond to the view presented in Text 1?
options: By agreeing that people cultivated wild wheat before domesticated forms appeared but denying that harvesting favored plants that retained their seeds
By arguing that wheat whose ears stay intact was already common in the wild before people began to cultivate cereals
By challenging the assumption that domesticated crops arose within a short time after people first began cultivating wild plants
By arguing that people who cultivated wild cereals went on living as mobile foragers for thousands of years
items.explanation: Text 1 describes a view in which domesticated crops “would emerge within a few centuries at most” after cultivation began. Tanno and Willcox found that cultivation of wild wheat “probably began around 10,500 years ago” but nonshattering forms “appeared only around 9,500 years ago,” and shattering forms “remained common in cultivated fields some 2,000 years later.” Their findings therefore challenge the idea that domestication followed quickly on cultivation.

A.recipe: D7 half right (true sequence, speed read as mechanism)
A.why_wrong: Text 2 does show cultivation beginning before domesticated wheat appeared, but it never denies that harvesting favored nonshattering plants; its point is that those plants “appeared only around 9,500 years ago,” long after cultivation began.

B.why_wrong: Text 2 says wild wheat shatters at maturity; the intact, nonshattering form is the domesticated one, and it appeared well after cultivation began, not before.

D.why_wrong: Text 2 shows that the plants changed slowly, not that the people kept a foraging way of life; it says nothing about how cultivators lived.

sources.what: Tanno and Willcox 2006, Science 311: previous estimates suggested rapid domestication; indehiscent (nonshattering) wheat emerged about 9,500 years BP and shattering forms were still common in cultivated fields about 7,500 BP; agriculture originated about 10,500 BP

items.notes: Area: natural and social science (archaeobotany). Framework: Childe’s “Neolithic Revolution” as a rapid break (well-known term). Key paraphrases at one level above the data (domesticated crops vs nonshattering ears). Abstract fetched via Europe PMC (PMID 16574859).

fixes: hardened A (its rebuttal half was killed by 'Near East') into true sequence plus a denial of the selection mechanism that Text 2 never makes
key C lengthened from 15 to 19 words (was well short of the 20-21 word distractors)

items.passage:
Text 1

Crows in Davis, California, have been reported to drop walnuts onto streets and eat the nutmeat after passing cars crush the shells. The behavior, first documented there in 1974, has frequently been presented as evidence of corvid ingenuity: the birds, according to this interpretation, deliberately position nuts where traffic will fracture shells that their beaks cannot.

Text 2

Daniel Cristol and colleagues observed walnut-eating crows along two Davis streets. The crows were no more likely to drop walnuts onto the road when a car was approaching than when none was, and departing birds were no more likely to abandon their nuts when cars approached. Crows also dropped walnuts on rooftops, sidewalks, and vacant parking lots. Moreover, the researchers noted, nuts crushed by cars stick to the pavement, where competitors quickly steal them.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would Cristol and colleagues (Text 2) most likely respond to the interpretation of the crows’ behavior presented in Text 1?
options: That behavior probably reflects the crows’ efforts to keep other birds from taking their walnuts, since a crushed nut is harder to defend.
That behavior shows that crows time their drops to approaching cars only on streets where traffic is heavy enough to make the effort worthwhile.
That behavior might be explained by the crows’ use of hard surfaces in general to open nuts, with cars cracking some shells only incidentally.
That behavior is genuine, but crows reserve it for nuts too hard to open by dropping them onto rooftops, sidewalks, or parking lots.
items.explanation: Text 1 presents the view that the crows “deliberately position nuts where traffic will fracture shells that their beaks cannot.” Cristol and colleagues found that the crows were “no more likely to drop walnuts onto the road when a car was approaching than when none was” and that they also dropped walnuts on “rooftops, sidewalks, and vacant parking lots.” This suggests that the crows simply use hard surfaces to open nuts and that cars crush some of them only by chance.

A.why_wrong: Text 2 mentions theft of crushed nuts as a drawback of having cars crack them, not as a reason crows drop nuts on roads; it does not say the crows are guarding their nuts.

B.why_wrong: Text 2 found no sign that crows time their drops to cars; it gives no result in which they do so on busier streets.

D.recipe: D7 half right (recycled detail, wrong conclusion)
D.why_wrong: Text 2 mentions rooftops, sidewalks, and parking lots to show that crows open nuts on hard surfaces of every kind, and it found the crows “no more likely to drop walnuts onto the road when a car was approaching than when none was,” so it gives no sign that crows aim any nuts at cars.

sources.what: Cristol, Switzer, Johnson and Walke 1997, The Auk 114(2): 296-298 (doi 10.2307/4089172), Davis, California: crows no more likely to arrive or drop walnuts when a car approached, no more likely to relinquish nuts; crows drop walnuts on rooftops, sidewalks, vacant parking lots; crushed nuts stick to the road and are stolen; interactions with cars incidental; original report Maple 1974

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal behavior). Full text read (archived SORA PDF). The paper has no abstract; the URL above is the full text. Text 1 is unattributed.

fixes: hardened D (unaddressed add-on about learning) into a half-right option that recycles Text 2's rooftops and parking lots
review.note: core claim read in the archived SORA PDF of Cristol et al. 1997 (no more likely to drop or relinquish nuts when cars approach; rooftops, sidewalks, parking lots; crushed nuts stolen)

items.passage:
Text 1

The fortified city of Carcassonne in southern France owes much of its present appearance to architect Eugène Viollet-le-Duc, who began restoring its ramparts in 1853. His restoration attracted criticism even during his lifetime, and justifiably: he capped numerous towers with pointed slate roofs characteristic of northern France rather than the terracotta tiles appropriate to the region’s climate and architectural traditions. Visitors therefore encounter towers belonging to a different region entirely.

Text 2

Had local opposition not overturned the French government’s 1849 decision to demolish Carcassonne’s walls, little would have survived to restore. Nevertheless, Viollet-le-Duc’s work there followed a principle he set out in 1858: to restore a building is “to re-establish it in a complete state which may never have existed at any given moment.” Visitors therefore experience less the fortress’s actual history than the architect’s idea of a perfect medieval stronghold.
items.stem: Which choice best describes a difference in how the authors of Text 1 and Text 2 view Viollet-le-Duc’s restoration of Carcassonne?
options: The author of Text 1 faults specific features for not suiting the region, whereas the author of Text 2 faults the restoration’s underlying goal of creating an idealized whole.
The author of Text 1 objects to the roofing materials used on many of the towers, whereas the author of Text 2 suggests that the walls would have been better left unrestored.
The author of Text 1 regards the restoration as a faithful record of medieval building practices, whereas the author of Text 2 regards it as largely the architect’s invention.
The author of Text 1 credits Viollet-le-Duc with saving the walls from demolition, whereas the author of Text 2 objects to towers more typical of northern France.
items.explanation: Both authors criticize the restoration, but on different grounds. The author of Text 1 objects to specific features, the “pointed slate roofs characteristic of northern France,” which do not suit “the region’s climate and architectural traditions.” The author of Text 2 objects to the principle behind the whole project, which aimed at “a complete state which may never have existed at any given moment,” so that visitors experience “the architect’s idea of a perfect medieval stronghold.”

B.why_wrong: The Text 1 half is accurate, but the author of Text 2 values the walls’ survival (“little would have survived to restore”) and never suggests they should have been left unrestored.

C.why_wrong: The Text 2 half fits, but the author of Text 1 says the restoration misrepresents the region’s building traditions, so it does not regard it as faithful.

D.why_wrong: This reverses the texts: it is Text 2 that mentions the walls’ rescue from demolition (and credits local protest, not Viollet-le-Duc), and Text 1 that objects to northern-style roofs.

sources.what: Cite de Carcassonne (Wikipedia): 1849 demolition decision opposed locally and reversed; restoration by Viollet-le-Duc began 1853; criticized in his lifetime for slate roofs suited to northern France rather than terracotta tiles
Viollet-le-Duc’s 1858 definition of restoration (Dictionnaire raisonné, vol. 8), quoted in translation

items.notes: Area: arts and history (architecture, restoration). Non-book object, two critiques on different grounds (3.10 pattern). Both texts are the authors’ own views; the facts they use are sourced.

items.passage:
Text 1

Most bats find their way in the dark by echolocation, producing calls in the larynx and analyzing the returning echoes. Old World fruit bats, a large family distributed from Africa to Australia, have traditionally been classified differently: they navigate primarily by vision and smell. <u>Apart from a few species of the genus Rousettus, which echolocate using tongue clicks, these bats possess no means of detecting objects through echoes.</u>

Text 2

Arjan Boonman, Sara Bumrungsri, and Yossi Yovel investigated how two fruit bat species classified as nonecholocating oriented themselves in complete darkness. Both species produced click-like sounds and used the returning echoes to detect and discriminate between objects. Remarkably, the clicks originated not from the bats’ mouths but from their wings. This echo sensing was rudimentary, however: unlike other echolocating bats, these species could not estimate distance accurately.
items.stem: Based on the texts, what would the researchers in Text 2 most likely say about the claim underlined in Text 1?
options: It is largely accurate, because the clicks the two species produced did not allow them to judge distance as other echolocating bats can.
It overstates the role of vision, because fruit bats depend mainly on their sense of smell to find their way.
It is mistaken about Rousettus, because those bats produce their echolocation clicks with their wings rather than their tongues.
It is too sweeping, because some fruit bats outside Rousettus can sense objects using echoes from clicks made with their wings.
items.explanation: Text 1 claims that, apart from a few Rousettus species, Old World fruit bats “possess no means of detecting objects through echoes.” Boonman and colleagues found that two species “classified as nonecholocating” made clicks with their wings and “used the returning echoes to detect and discriminate between objects.” The researchers would therefore say the claim is too broad.

A.why_wrong: Text 2 does say the bats could not judge distance, but they still used echoes “to detect and discriminate between objects,” which is exactly what the claim says they cannot do.

B.why_wrong: Neither text compares the roles of vision and smell; the underlined claim is about sensing objects through echoes.

C.why_wrong: Text 2 says nothing about Rousettus; the wing clicks came from two species classified as nonecholocating, and Text 1 says Rousettus clicks with its tongue.

sources.what: Boonman, Bumrungsri and Yovel 2014, Current Biology 24(24): two Old World fruit bat species classified as nonecholocating used click-based echo sensing in complete darkness; rudimentary, could not estimate distance accurately; clicks generated with the wings, unlike laryngeal or tongue clicks of other echolocating bats

items.notes: Area: natural science (sensory biology). Counterexample to an ‘only/apart from’ claim. Rousettus tongue clicks and the family’s range are background knowledge, simplified. Abstract fetched via Europe PMC (PMID 25484290).

items.passage:
Text 1

The finest walls of Cusco, the Inca capital in present-day Peru, consist of massive stone blocks fitted together without mortar, their joints so precise that they are barely visible. Because the Inca lacked iron tools, some writers have concluded that <u>such precision could not have been achieved with the rudimentary implements available to Inca builders</u>, proposing instead forgotten techniques, such as plant extracts that softened the stone.

Text 2

During the 1980s, architect Jean-Pierre Protzen investigated Inca quarries near Ollantaytambo and examined numerous cut-stone walls. Blocks, he determined, were pried from rock faces or selected from rockfalls, then shaped by pounding with hammerstones; each new block was fitted by trimming previously laid stones to receive it, through trial and error. Protzen’s experiments demonstrated that with these methods stones could be cut, dressed, and fitted with little effort and in a short time.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the underlined claim in Text 1?
options: The Inca most likely acquired iron tools through trade with peoples living beyond the borders of their empire.
The tight fit of Inca masonry could probably have been achieved with the tools and methods available to the Inca.
Inca builders preferred stones from rockfalls because quarrying rock faces was too difficult for them.
The walls in Cusco were probably finished by Spanish builders after the empire fell.
items.explanation: Text 1 reports the claim that the precision of Inca walls “could not have been achieved with the rudimentary implements available to Inca builders.” Text 2 describes how blocks were “shaped by pounding with hammerstones” and fitted “through trial and error,” and notes that Protzen’s experiments demonstrated that stones “could be cut, dressed, and fitted with little effort and in a short time.” So the author of Text 2 would say such precision was achievable with the means the Inca had.

A.why_wrong: Neither text suggests that the Inca obtained iron tools; Text 2’s point is that stone hammers were enough.

C.why_wrong: Text 2 says blocks were either “pried from rock faces or selected from rockfalls”; it never says quarrying was too difficult.

D.why_wrong: Neither text mentions Spanish builders; Text 2 explains how the Inca themselves could have fitted the stones.

sources.what: Protzen 1985, Journal of the Society of Architectural Historians 44(2), Inca Quarrying and Stonecutting: wild speculation about Inca techniques; stones taken from rockfalls or broken from rock faces with pry-bars, split and dressed with hammerstones, fitted by cutting already laid stones by trial and error; experiments show little effort and short time
Protzen’s fieldwork at Ollantaytambo quarries from 1982

items.notes: Area: social science and history (archaeology, architecture). Abstract read via Crossref. Statement-shell options as in 2.4.

items.passage:
Text 1

For decades, water agencies in the arid western United States have seeded winter clouds over mountains, dispersing particles of silver iodide on which ice crystals can form. Because snowfall varies enormously from storm to storm, the technique’s effectiveness has been evaluated mainly through statistical comparisons of seeded and unseeded storms. <u>Proponents nonetheless regard cloud seeding as a dependable way to add substantially to the snowpack that replenishes the region’s rivers and reservoirs.</u>

Text 2

In 2017, atmospheric scientist Katja Friedrich and colleagues used radar to isolate snowfall that could be attributed unambiguously to cloud seeding over mountains in Idaho. The seeding clearly worked: snow formed within the seeded clouds and reached the ground. Yet precipitation gauges recorded increases of only 0.05 to 0.3 millimeters, a fraction of a millimeter of water, as the seeded snow passed over them.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the underlined portion of Text 1?
options: By arguing that statistical comparisons of storms have exaggerated how often seeding produces any additional snow
By suggesting that the particles released during seeding do little to help ice crystals form in winter clouds
By suggesting that seeding may yield real but rather modest amounts of additional snow
By noting that radar cannot reliably distinguish snow produced by seeding from snow that falls naturally
items.explanation: Text 1 reports proponents’ view that seeding can “add substantially to the snowpack.” The author of Text 2 grants that “The seeding clearly worked” but stresses that gauges “recorded increases of only 0.05 to 0.3 millimeters.” The author would therefore suggest that seeding produces real but limited amounts of snow.

A.why_wrong: Text 2 does not evaluate the earlier statistical comparisons or say how often seeding works; it reports cases in which seeding clearly did produce snow.

B.why_wrong: Text 2 says “The seeding clearly worked,” so it would not claim that the particles do little to help snow form.

D.why_wrong: Text 2 reports the reverse: radar was used to isolate snowfall “that could be attributed unambiguously to cloud seeding.”

sources.what: Friedrich et al. 2020, PNAS 117(10) (SNOWIE): for over half a century cloud seeding evaluated statistically; radar isolates precipitation unambiguously attributed to seeding; gauges measured increases of 0.05 to 0.3 mm; water generated 100 to 275 acre-feet in three cases

items.notes: Area: natural science (atmospheric science). Stem speaker is the author of Text 2, whose word “only” carries the limit. SNOWIE took place in Idaho in early 2017 (background, simplified). Abstract fetched via Europe PMC (PMID 32094189).

items.passage:
Text 1

Online ratings promise to aggregate the judgments of many individuals, but they may be susceptible to herding. When people can observe how others have evaluated an item before rating it themselves, early judgments can influence later ones, so that an initial surge of approval or disapproval gathers momentum. <u>According to this view, a few early votes, whether favorable or unfavorable, can permanently distort an item’s reputation.</u>

Text 2

Lev Muchnik, Sinan Aral, and Sean Taylor conducted a randomized experiment on a news-aggregation website, assigning comments a single up-vote or down-vote at random immediately after they were posted. An initial up-vote made the next viewer 32 percent more likely to rate the comment positively, and such comments accumulated final ratings 25 percent higher, on average, than comparable comments. Down-voted comments, by contrast, tended to be corrected by subsequent users.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would Muchnik, Aral, and Taylor (Text 2) most likely respond to the view presented in the underlined sentence in Text 1?
options: By suggesting that early votes may push later ratings upward but are much less likely to drag them down
By arguing that most viewers disregard others’ ratings when deciding how to rate an item themselves
By pointing out that unfavorable early votes have a more lasting effect on ratings than favorable ones do
By noting that herding occurs mainly when viewers are personally acquainted with the people whose ratings they see
items.explanation: Text 1 holds that early votes, “whether favorable or unfavorable,” can permanently distort an item’s reputation. Muchnik, Aral, and Taylor found that an initial up-vote raised later ratings, with comments accumulating final ratings “25 percent higher, on average,” but that “Down-voted comments, by contrast, tended to be corrected by subsequent users.” They would therefore say the effect holds for favorable early votes but not for unfavorable ones.

B.why_wrong: An initial up-vote made the next viewer “32 percent more likely to rate the comment positively,” so viewers clearly did not disregard others’ ratings.

C.why_wrong: Text 2 found the opposite: up-votes had a lasting effect, while down-voted comments “tended to be corrected.”

D.why_wrong: Neither text discusses whether viewers know the people whose ratings they see.

sources.what: Muchnik, Aral and Taylor 2013, Science 341: randomized experiment on a social news aggregation site; positive manipulation raised the likelihood of positive ratings by 32 percent and final ratings by 25 percent on average; negative social influence was corrected by users

items.notes: Area: social science (online behavior). Limit of scope: herding in one direction only. The study manipulated votes on comments (background, simplified). Abstract fetched via Europe PMC (PMID 23929980).

items.passage:
Text 1

In 1971, petroleum engineers analyzing auctions for offshore oil leases described a phenomenon now known as the winner’s curse. When numerous bidders compete for an item whose true value is uncertain, each must estimate that value, and the highest bid tends to come from whoever overestimated it most. Consequently, even when bidders’ estimates are accurate on average, the winner frequently pays more than the item ultimately proves to be worth.

Text 2

Each year, National Football League teams take turns selecting promising college players in a draft, and teams frequently surrender several later selections in order to move up and choose earlier. Researchers Cade Massey and Richard Thaler compared the cost of early picks, in traded selections and in players’ salaries, with the value the chosen players actually provide. Top picks, they found, are significantly overvalued, a pattern inconsistent with efficient markets.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 1 most likely respond to the findings presented in Text 2?
options: By arguing that the findings are surprising, since teams with long experience in drafting players should not consistently overpay
By suggesting that the teams willing to pay the most to move up in the draft may be those that most overestimate the players available
By pointing out that a draft differs from an auction because football teams cannot simply use money to bid against one another for the players they want
By claiming that football teams, unlike bidders for oil leases, tend to estimate the value of what they acquire accurately on average
items.explanation: Text 1 explains that when bidders compete for an item of uncertain value, “the highest bid tends to come from whoever overestimated it most,” so winners often overpay. Text 2 reports that teams “surrender several later selections” to move up and that top picks are “significantly overvalued.” The author of Text 1 would see this as the winner’s curse at work: the teams that pay the most for early picks may be the ones that most overestimate the players.

A.why_wrong: Text 1’s author explains overpaying as a built-in result of competitive bidding, even when estimates are “accurate on average,” so the findings would not seem surprising.

C.why_wrong: Neither text argues that the draft cannot be compared with an auction; Text 2 notes that teams pay for picks with other selections and with salaries.

D.why_wrong: This reuses Text 1’s phrase about estimates being accurate on average to set football teams against oil bidders, a contrast neither text draws.

sources.what: Massey and Thaler 2013, Management Science 59(7), The Loser’s Curse: NFL draft-day trades, player performance and compensation; top draft picks significantly overvalued, inconsistent with rational expectations and efficient markets

items.notes: Area: social science (behavioral economics). Text 1 frame (winner’s curse, Capen, Clapp and Campbell 1971 on offshore oil-lease bidding) is textbook background; the core claim is Text 2’s. Text 1 speaks about Text 2’s case. Abstract fetched via OpenAlex.

fixes: lengthened C so the key is not the longest option (medium key-longest rate was 5 of 9 against CB's 4 of 11)

items.passage:
Text 1

When naturalist Georg Wilhelm Steller was shipwrecked on Bering Island in 1741, he described an enormous, slow-moving marine mammal that grazed on kelp around the Commander Islands, its only remaining habitat. Fur traders and seal hunters following the route of Steller’s expedition soon began stopping at the islands to slaughter the animals for their meat and fat. By 1768, Steller’s sea cow had been hunted to extinction.

Text 2

Ecologist James Estes and colleagues argue that hunting explains only part of the extinction. During those same decades, the fur trade drastically reduced sea otter populations around the islands. Because otters prey on sea urchins, their disappearance typically allows urchin populations to multiply and devour kelp forests—the sea cow’s food supply. Even if no sea cow had been killed directly, the researchers conclude, the loss of otters and kelp would probably have doomed the species.
items.stem: Based on the texts, the author of Text 1 and Estes and colleagues (Text 2) would most likely agree with which statement?
options: Steller’s sea cows were hunted mainly for their hides rather than their meat.
Steller’s sea cows would probably have survived if hunting had stopped soon after 1741.
Steller’s sea cows competed with sea otters for the sea urchins that lived among the kelp around the islands.
The arrival of the fur trade in the region contributed to the disappearance of Steller’s sea cow.
items.explanation: The texts disagree about how the sea cow died out, but both tie its end to the fur trade. Text 1 says that “Fur traders and seal hunters” killed the animals until they were “hunted to extinction,” and Text 2 says the fur trade “drastically reduced sea otter populations,” setting off the loss of the kelp the sea cows ate. Both would therefore agree that the fur trade contributed to the species’ disappearance.

A.why_wrong: Text 1 says the animals were killed “for their meat and fat”; neither text says they were hunted mainly for their hides.

B.why_wrong: The author of Text 1 might accept this, but Estes and colleagues argue that the loss of otters and kelp “would probably have doomed the species” even without direct killing.

C.why_wrong: Text 2 says otters prey on urchins and sea cows ate kelp; neither text says sea cows ate urchins or competed with otters.

sources.what: Estes, Burdin and Doak 2016, PNAS 113(4): sea cows at the Commander Islands when Europeans arrived in 1741; extinction during the early maritime fur trade widely attributed to overkill, but loss of sea otters and kelp a probable cause even without direct killing
Text 1 details: Steller 1741, Bering Island, range limited to Commander Islands, hunted for meat and fat by fur traders, extinct by 1768

items.notes: Area: natural science (ecology, extinction). Rival causes, shared premise stated one level more abstractly (the fur trade contributed). Abstract fetched via Europe PMC (PMID 26504217).

fixes: A why_wrong: cut an unsourced claim that only the fur trade was about hides
lengthened C so the key is not the longest option

items.passage:
Text 1

In 1760, the Scottish poet James Macpherson published English versions of poems that he claimed to have collected in the Highlands and translated from Gaelic. The following year he announced the discovery of an entire epic, Fingal, attributed to a third-century bard named Ossian. The minister and critic Hugh Blair, a firm believer in the poems’ authenticity, raised funds to support Macpherson’s further Gaelic research and championed the poems as genuine relics of an ancient oral tradition.

Text 2

Doubts arose almost immediately, and Macpherson was never able to substantiate his claims about where the poems came from. Scholars now generally conclude that Macpherson composed the Ossian poems largely himself, although he drew in part on traditional Gaelic poetry that he had collected. Whatever their origins, the poems were translated into the major European languages and profoundly influenced the Romantic movement.
items.stem: Based on the texts, Hugh Blair (Text 1) and the scholars described in Text 2 would most likely agree with which statement?
options: Macpherson’s poems are faithful translations of works composed by a third-century bard named Ossian.
Macpherson invented the Ossian poems without drawing on any existing Gaelic poetry or stories.
Gaelic material that Macpherson collected in Scotland contributed at least in part to the Ossian poems.
The Ossian poems had a greater influence on writers elsewhere in Europe than on writers in Scotland.
items.explanation: Blair and the modern scholars disagree about how authentic the poems are, but both accept that Macpherson worked from Gaelic material he had gathered. Blair believed the poems were genuine works that Macpherson had “collected in the Highlands and translated from Gaelic,” and the scholars in Text 2 hold that Macpherson “drew in part on traditional Gaelic poetry that he had collected.” Both would therefore agree that Gaelic material he collected in Scotland contributed at least in part to the poems.

A.why_wrong: Blair, “a firm believer in the poems’ authenticity,” might accept this, but the scholars in Text 2 conclude that Macpherson “composed the Ossian poems largely himself.”

B.why_wrong: Blair believed the poems were genuine, and the scholars say Macpherson “drew in part on traditional Gaelic poetry,” so neither party holds that he used no Gaelic sources.

D.why_wrong: Text 2 says the poems were translated widely and influenced the Romantic movement, but neither text compares their influence in Scotland with their influence elsewhere.

sources.what: Ossian (Wikipedia): Macpherson claimed to have collected Gaelic material and translated it (Fingal 1761); current consensus that he largely composed the poems himself, drawing in part on traditional Gaelic poetry he had collected; translated into the literary languages of Europe; influential on Romanticism

Text 1 and 2 details: 1760 Fragments of Ancient Poetry; Hugh Blair a firm believer in authenticity who raised a subscription for Macpherson’s Gaelic research; authenticity challenged at once and none of Macpherson’s claims substantiated

items.notes: Area: literature (literary history, authorship dispute). Shared premise beneath an authenticity dispute. Replaced a sweet potato draft whose study is already used in an official Inferences item.

fixes: saturated theme: cut Text 2's 'errors in chronology and in the forms of Gaelic names' (the anachronism-exposure trope) so the item reads as a partial-authenticity dispute, not a fake exposed by an anachronism; replaced with the sourced 'never able to substantiate his claims'
options lengthened toward the medium mean (11-13 words to 14-17), key hedged 'at least in part'
review.note: forgery theme judged: the item tests a shared premise (collected Gaelic material), and with the anachronism clause cut it no longer reads like the live forgery items (Grolier Codex, Galileo sheet)

items.passage:
Text 1

The Hawaiian Islands and the Emperor Seamounts form a volcanic chain extending across the Pacific Ocean, its volcanoes progressively older with increasing distance from Hawaii. Geologists have long interpreted the chain as the track of a hotspot anchored deep in Earth’s mantle, over which the Pacific plate has gradually moved. According to this interpretation, the chain’s sharp bend, dating to approximately 47 million years ago, records an abrupt change in the direction of plate motion.

Text 2

Geophysicist John Tarduno and colleagues analyzed lava samples drilled from several Emperor Seamounts. Magnetic minerals in lava preserve the latitude at which it solidified, and the samples revealed a consistent pattern: the older the seamount, the farther north it had formed, considerably north of Hawaii’s present latitude. The researchers concluded that between approximately 81 and 47 million years ago, the hotspot itself migrated rapidly southward, and that this motion principally formed the Emperor chain.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would Tarduno and colleagues (Text 2) most likely respond to the explanation of the bend presented in Text 1?
options: By arguing that it fails to account for evidence of where the Emperor Seamounts’ lavas originally formed
By insisting that it underestimates how old the volcanoes at the northern end of the chain are
By concurring that the plate changed direction but disputing that it did so 47 million years ago
By agreeing that hotspots stay fixed in the mantle while the plates above them move
items.explanation: Text 1 explains the bend as the result of a change in the motion of a plate passing over a fixed hotspot. Tarduno and colleagues found that magnetic minerals showed “the older the seamount, the farther north it had formed,” and they concluded that “the hotspot itself migrated rapidly southward.” They would therefore say that the fixed-hotspot explanation does not account for the latitudes recorded in the seamounts’ lavas.

B.why_wrong: Text 2 uses the seamounts’ ages but never says Text 1 has them wrong; its objection concerns where the lavas formed.

C.why_wrong: Text 2 accepts the 47-million-year date (its hotspot motion ends then) and attributes the chain’s shape to hotspot motion rather than conceding a change in plate direction.

D.why_wrong: Tarduno and colleagues conclude that “the hotspot itself migrated,” so they reject the idea of a fixed hotspot.

sources.what: Tarduno et al. 2003, Science 301: the bend was the basis for a fixed-hotspot change in plate motion; paleomagnetic and radiometric data from drilled Emperor Seamount samples show age-progressive paleolatitudes; trend formed principally by rapid motion of the Hawaiian plume from 81 to 47 million years ago

items.notes: Area: natural science (geophysics). Rival hypothesis with evidence the target does not account for (2.5 pattern, different option wording). Abstract fetched via Europe PMC (PMID 12881572).

items.passage:
Text 1

Thousands of the world’s languages may fall silent within this century, many of them spoken by small communities in remote areas. Documenting a language has traditionally required trained linguists to travel to a community, record speakers, and then spend many hours transcribing and translating the recordings. Because endangered languages far outnumber the linguists able to do this work, many are likely to disappear before they can be documented.

Text 2

In 2014, linguist Steven Bird and colleagues introduced Aikuma, a smartphone app for documenting languages. Aikuma is designed to put the central tasks of language documentation—recording speech, respeaking it slowly and carefully so that it can later be transcribed, and translating it orally into a more widely spoken language—in the hands of members of a speech community themselves. Recordings made on one phone can be shared with other phones.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the problem presented in Text 1?
options: By recommending that linguists concentrate on languages that still have many speakers
By noting that speakers themselves may be able to do work that has depended on visiting linguists
By suggesting that transcribing recordings is no longer needed to document a language
By identifying additional reasons that small communities in remote areas may hesitate to have their languages recorded by outsiders
items.explanation: Text 1 identifies a problem: documentation depends on linguists, and there are too few of them for the many endangered languages. Text 2 describes an app designed to put recording, respeaking, and translating “in the hands of members of a speech community themselves.” The author of Text 2 would therefore point to a way for speakers to do work that once required visiting linguists.

A.why_wrong: Text 2 offers a way to document more languages, not advice to shift attention to languages that are less endangered.

C.why_wrong: Text 2 says speech is respoken “so that it can later be transcribed,” so transcription is still part of the process.

D.why_wrong: Neither text suggests that communities are reluctant to be recorded; Text 2 presents a solution, not further difficulties.

sources.what: Bird, Hanke, Adams and Lee 2014, Aikuma: A Mobile App for Collaborative Language Documentation (ACL workshop on computational methods for endangered languages): app puts recording, respeaking and translating in the hands of a speech community; networked recording device

items.notes: Area: social science (linguistics). Problem and solution (2.11 pattern). Abstract fetched via OpenAlex (doi 10.3115/v1/W14-2201). Text 1 figures left general.

fixes: lengthened D so the key is not the longest option

items.passage:
Text 1

Viewers trained in European art sometimes find Chinese landscape scrolls puzzling. Since the Renaissance, European painters have generally used linear perspective, which presents a scene as it would appear to someone standing at one fixed point. Judged by that standard, a painting in which the viewer seems to look up at a mountain’s peaks while also looking down into its valleys can appear inconsistent, as if the painter had not mastered depth.

Text 2

Guo Xi, a court painter of China’s Northern Song dynasty, created landscapes such as Early Spring (1072) that combine multiple viewpoints. This approach, sometimes called “floating perspective,” frees the eye to travel through the landscape. Guo Xi even named his method of combining views “the angle of totality.” It was an alternative way of representing space, not a failed attempt at the European one.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely regard the judgment of Chinese landscape painting described in Text 1?
options: As unfair, because European painters of the same period also combined several viewpoints in their landscapes
As outdated, because Chinese painters in later centuries began using linear perspective in their work
As reasonable, because Guo Xi’s paintings were meant to be viewed only by members of the court
As misguided, because the combined viewpoints in such paintings were a deliberate technique rather than a mistake
items.explanation: Text 1 describes viewers who judge Chinese landscapes by the standard of linear perspective and conclude that the painter “had not mastered depth.” The author of Text 2 explains that Guo Xi combined viewpoints on purpose, naming his method “the angle of totality,” and calls it “an alternative way of representing space, not a failed attempt at the European one.” The author would therefore regard the judgment as misguided.

A.why_wrong: Text 2 might call the judgment unfair, but it never says European painters combined viewpoints; its reason is that the Chinese method was deliberate.

B.why_wrong: Neither text says Chinese painters later adopted linear perspective.

C.why_wrong: Text 2 disagrees with the judgment, and neither text says who was allowed to view Guo Xi’s paintings.

sources.what: Guo Xi (c. 1020 to c. 1090), Northern Song court painter; Early Spring (1072) shows multiple perspectives he called the angle of totality, also called floating perspective, displacing the viewer’s static eye

items.notes: Area: arts (painting). As-adjective shell with D6 distractors (1.7 pattern); the critique is of a standard (single-point perspective) rather than of a genre’s history, so the frame differs from bluegrass.

items.passage:
Text 1

Bossa nova, the musical style that emerged in Rio de Janeiro during the late 1950s, owes its distinctive sound primarily to guitarist and singer João Gilberto. Gilberto adapted one rhythmic layer of a samba percussion ensemble for the guitar, plucking a simplified samba beat with his fingers. On his 1959 album Chega de Saudade, that guitar pattern became the foundation of an entirely new style.

Text 2

Gilberto’s guitar may be bossa nova’s signature, but the music’s character derived equally from the songs he performed. Composer Antônio Carlos Jobim, collaborating with lyricist Vinicius de Moraes on compositions such as “Chega de Saudade,” introduced sophisticated new harmonies to the samba song. Without Jobim’s compositions, Gilberto’s innovative rhythm would have had far less to carry.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
options: Bossa nova became popular in the United States before it became popular in Brazil.
Bossa nova’s guitar rhythm mattered more to its sound than its harmonies did.
Bossa nova was built in part on musical elements drawn from samba.
Gilberto rarely performed the songs that Jobim composed with Vinicius de Moraes.
items.explanation: The authors disagree about what mattered most in bossa nova, but both link it to samba. Text 1 says Gilberto played “a simplified samba beat,” and Text 2 says Jobim “introduced sophisticated new harmonies to the samba song.” Both would therefore agree that bossa nova was built in part on musical elements drawn from samba.

A.why_wrong: Neither text discusses bossa nova’s popularity in the United States.

B.why_wrong: The author of Text 1 might agree, but the author of Text 2 argues that the music’s character “derived equally from the songs he performed.”

D.why_wrong: Text 2 says the music’s character “derived equally from the songs he performed,” naming Jobim and de Moraes’s “Chega de Saudade,” which is also the title of Gilberto’s album in Text 1.

sources.what: Bossa nova (Wikipedia): emerged in Rio de Janeiro in the late 1950s; Gilberto extracted the bossa beat from samba percussion (tamborim layer) for the guitar; 1959 album Chega de Saudade; harmonies of Tom Jobim and lyrics of Vinicius de Moraes

items.notes: Area: arts (music). Same premise, different emphasis (1.2 pattern).

fixes: options were 14/13/8/8 words; lengthened C (key) and D to 12 words each
